title: Would a "sprite -> 3D model you can paint pixel-by-pixel" tool be useful to you?
author: EndOne6219
selftext:
Hi! I'm working on a small Windows tool (working name: Pictor) and before I go further I'd like to know if this is something you'd actually use. Screenshots attached.



What it does right now:

\- You give it a character sprite (front, and side/back/top if you have them).

\- Shape mode: you mark the sprite's pixels with body-part brushes (head, torso, arms, legs), press Inflate, and it builds a 3D shape that matches the sprite from every view. A red/blue guide shows where the model and the sprite don't match.

\- Skin mode: the model gets a texture you paint pixel by pixel, while a pixel-art view of the model sits next to the sprite, so you can match them exactly. You can also "spray" the sprite's colors onto the model.

\- The model can then be turned to any angle and still looks like pixel art (outlines, cel-style highlights).

\- Optional AI helpers: an AI agent that fixes the shape or paints the texture, PixelLab for extra views of the sprite, and "Skins": write a prompt and it re-textures the model into variants you pick from a grid.

\- Assets are grouped in projects (characters, furniture, tiles, hair).



What I'd like to know:

1. Would this be useful in your workflow? For what (more directions, animation, consistent characters…)?

2. What's missing that would make you actually use it?

3. Would you prefer it as a standalone app or as a plugin (Aseprite, Godot, Blender…)?



It's still early and rough. Honest opinions welcome, including "I wouldn't use this".

https://i.redd.it/fm10no50c12i1.png

https://i.redd.it/1z0zzy54c12i1.png

comments.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
comments.body:
One test I'd try: start with a front-only sprite that has an asymmetric detail (say, a shield on one arm), then compare the generated side view with a separately drawn reference. That would show where the missing view had to be guessed and whether a manual correction survives another generation.



For a game handoff, I'd prioritize a standalone export to fixed-size transparent sprite sheets with a consistent foot anchor before an engine-specific plugin. That gives the angles a common handoff and helps prevent the character jumping between frames.

replies.author: EndOne6219
replies.body:
Thanks, that's a good test! The workflow here is a bit different though: you first build the base character (the "mannequin") from the sprite, and then each piece like a shield or a weapon would be its own part attached to the mesh, not guessed from the front view. Attaching pieces is planned (it's the "Dress Room" part), it isn't in yet.

The fixed-size transparent sprite sheet export with a consistent foot anchor is a really good point, I'll put that before any engine plugin. Thanks!

replies.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
replies.body: Thanks for clarifying—I treated the shield as part of the base shape. A mannequin with one arm noticeably larger than the other would be a cleaner test of the inferred side view; the shield could instead test whether attaching equipment shifts the exported foot anchor once Dress Room is ready.

replies.author: EndOne6219
replies.body:
Arms are actually already covered: the sprite is always in a T-pose, so each arm is seen whole from the front and gets its own size, even if one is much bigger than the other (the top/bottom views give the arms their thickness).

The weak spot is the legs: their thickness comes from the profile, and the same profile is used for both legs. If you also give it the other side sprite (east as well as west), that's solved too.

And yes, the shield is a good test for the foot anchor once Dress Room is in. Thanks!

comments.author: Ferniclestix
comments.body:
hey if your doing this stuff, think about including model swaps, that way you can do stuff like hand poses, partial model changes, armor, that kind of stuff and it gets built in and it doesnt mess with your existingmodel, uses the same weights for rigs or animations or whtever.  
doing image swaps on my own program at the moment so i thought id mention it lol.

replies.author: EndOne6219
replies.body: That’s pretty much what I have in mind for the Dress Room part (still WIP). The idea is that armor and clothes are separate pieces fitted onto the base body, using the same skeleton and weights, so they follow any animation and the base model stays untouched. Hand poses as swappable parts is a great idea, I hadn’t thought of that one.
